Victory Gardens (US)

Household & community food gardensFor the peoplePartial / legacy
Where: Washington, US
Helped people provide their own: Vegetables
Period: 1917–18; 1941–45
Promoted by: US government
With farm labour, canned goods and rail capacity all diverted to feeding troops and allies in wartime, the government urged citizens to grow vegetables in yards, vacant lots and city parks; at the WWII peak these home gardens grew a large share of America’s fresh vegetables, easing shortages, freeing commercial supply for the military and giving the home front a tangible way to contribute.
Still around today: Ended as a national program after WWII, but the idea never died: it lives on in the US community-garden movement and resurfaced in the 2020 pandemic ‘victory garden’ boom.

Dig for Victory (UK)

Household & community food gardensFor the peoplePartial / legacy
Where: London, GB
Helped people provide their own: Household & allotment food
Period: 1939–45
Promoted by: UK government
Because Britain imported well over half its food and U-boats were sinking the ships that carried it, the government turned lawns, parks, football pitches and railway verges into vegetable plots and roughly doubled the number of allotments — growing food at home as a direct answer to the threat of being starved into surrender.
Still around today: The wartime scheme was wound down after 1945, but its legacy is Britain’s enduring allotment system and recurring ‘grow your own’ campaigns.

Household & community food gardensFor the peoplePartial / legacy
Where: Moscow, RU
Helped people provide their own: Family food
Period: 1930s–1991
Promoted by: Soviet state (tolerated)
Even under collectivised farming, families were allowed small private garden and dacha plots, which the state tolerated as a safety valve because the collective farms chronically underperformed; these household plots ended up producing a strikingly large share of the country’s potatoes, vegetables, fruit and eggs and keeping families fed when the planned system fell short.
Still around today: The USSR is gone, yet dacha gardening remains a mass habit across Russia and the former Soviet states, still supplying a real share of household food.

When the Soviet bloc collapsed and Cuba lost the oil, fertiliser and food imports it had depended on almost overnight, city lots, rooftops and patios across the island were turned into intensive organic gardens and neighbourhood market-gardens — growing food inside the cities being the only way to avert mass hunger during the ‘Special Period’.
Still around today: Still active and institutionalised — urban agriculture remains a significant, officially backed food source in Cuban cities today.

Still around today: Ended with the war, but Switzerland still keeps strong food-security planning and mandatory emergency stockpiles — the cultivation drive itself is history.

Amid the economic collapse that followed the USSR’s fall — hyperinflation, unpaid wages and a broken food-distribution system — the government widened access to garden and dacha plots, and tens of millions of families survived the chaos largely by growing their own potatoes and vegetables.
Still around today: The acute 1990s crisis passed, but dacha and garden food-growing continues widely — now more habit and supplement than survival.

Still around today: Very much alive: allotments remain legally protected, heavily used, and have long waiting lists across Britain.

Still around today: The campaigns ended, but home canning persists as a hobby and preparedness practice, with a notable resurgence in recent years.

Where: York, GB

Period: c. 8th–18th c.
Promoted by: Manorial communities
Across medieval Europe villagers farmed scattered strips in open fields and grazed livestock, gathered wood and foraged on shared common land — an arrangement that let peasant households feed themselves even as it sat inside a manorial order that extracted their labour and dues; centuries later, enclosure dismantled it.
Still around today: Partial — most commons were enclosed by the 19th century, but registered commons and commoners’ rights still survive in places such as England and Switzerland.

The Russian peasant commune (mir) periodically repartitioned village land among households so each family had enough to live on for its size — a subsistence-levelling system the state also leaned on as its unit for collecting taxes and recruits, serving ruler and ruled at once.
Still around today: Defunct — undermined by Stolypin’s reforms and then replaced by Soviet collective farms; gone as an institution.

Promoted by: PRC (Mao era)
Maoist self-reliance hardened after the Sino-Soviet split abruptly cut off Soviet aid and advisers, and under the slogan ‘in agriculture, learn from Dazhai’ rural communes were urged to feed themselves, build their own terraces and infrastructure and rely on their own labour — making village-level self-sufficiency both a doctrine and a practical necessity.
Still around today: Defunct: the communes were dismantled after 1978 with the return to household farming, and Dazhai itself is now mostly a tourist and heritage site.

Promoted by: South Korea (Park Chung-hee)
As South Korea’s cities industrialised and the countryside fell behind, the state launched a ‘New Village’ movement built on diligence, self-reliance and cooperation, in which villages organised to build their own roads, housing, water and incomes through collective self-help backed by small government matching grants — pushing villages to lift themselves rather than wait for handouts.
Still around today: Still exists through Saemaul organisations and is now actively exported abroad as a rural-development model, though its 1970s heyday has passed.

Promoted by: Tanzania (Nyerere)
Following Nyerere’s Arusha Declaration and its creed of ‘self-reliance’ (kujitegemea) — meant to keep a poor new nation from depending on foreign aid or capital — millions of Tanzanians were gathered into communal ‘ujamaa’ villages designed to farm collectively and provide for their own food and basic needs, a deliberate doctrine of grassroots independence more than a response to any single crisis.
Still around today: Abandoned in the mid-1980s after the policy failed economically; the villages remain but the communal self-reliance program is over.

Still around today: Partial — the Inca state and mit’a are gone, but the ayllu survives as a living communal institution in Andean villages today.

Still around today: Still exist (~270 kibbutzim), but most have privatised since the 1990s and are no longer self-sufficient communes.
